narrative:
The model determined that you have a 74% chance of failing the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability is well above the school's acceptance threshold, your law school application was rejected.

The decision was driven primarily by three factors from your academic record. Your first-year and third-year class rankings were the strongest influences, both pushing the prediction strongly toward failure. You placed in the bottom decile of your class in both years, compared with an average around the middle of the pack among students who were accepted. These low rankings signaled to the model that you would likely struggle with the demands of law school and the bar exam.

Your LSAT score was the third most important factor, but it worked in the opposite direction. At 34, your score is a bit below the 37 average of accepted students, yet it still provided a modest pull toward passing. Unfortunately, this positive influence was not large enough to offset the much stronger negative signals from your class rankings.

The model did not consider your gender or race in any way. Your family income, undergraduate GPA, and plan to attend full-time played only minor roles.

To improve your chances, focus on raising your academic performance and retaking the LSAT to demonstrate stronger readiness. Many students successfully reapply after strengthening these areas. Consider academic support programs or a prep course before your next attempt.
